How many letters are there in the Devanagari alphabet?
entities.prompt: How many letters are there in the Devanagari alphabet?
entities.explanation: 44 — each with one sound. That finite size is why the alphabet comes first: once you know the letters you can read anything.

entities.title: Why is the alphabet the right place to start, before vocabulary?
entities.prompt: Why is the alphabet the right place to start, before vocabulary?
options: Hindi is written in English letters
entities.explanation: Because Hindi is phonetic and finite. Two or three weeks on the letters and you can sound out any word, which makes vocabulary easier, not harder.

entities.title: What does the guide give you to help the letters stick?
entities.prompt: What does the guide give you to help the letters stick?
entities.answer: A printable chart and a learning order
options: A printable chart and a learning order
entities.explanation: A printable chart and the order to learn the letters in — pin the chart up and work through the letters in that order.

entities.title: Is namaste always the right greeting?
entities.prompt: Is namaste always the right greeting?
entities.answer: No — sometimes it is the wrong word
options: No — sometimes it is the wrong word
entities.explanation: No — it is sometimes the wrong word. Which greeting to use changes by time of day, age, religion and situation.

entities.title: Which of these is a time-of-day greeting?
entities.prompt: Which of these is a time-of-day greeting?
entities.explanation: सुप्रभात (suprabhat) — good morning. Namaste is general; suprabhat is only for the morning.

entities.title: What matters more than the greeting itself?
entities.prompt: What matters more than the greeting itself?
entities.explanation: The follow-up question — asking how the person is — which matters more than which greeting you opened with.

entities.title: Where does the verb go in a Hindi sentence?
entities.prompt: Where does the verb go in a Hindi sentence?
entities.explanation: At the end — Hindi is subject-object-verb, so the action is the last thing you hear.

entities.title: What does Hindi use instead of English prepositions like “in” and “on”?
entities.prompt: What does Hindi use instead of English prepositions like “in” and “on”?
entities.explanation: Postpositions — small words that go AFTER the noun, not before it.

entities.title: Why do Hindi sentences feel “backwards” at first?
entities.prompt: Why do Hindi sentences feel “backwards” at first?
options: Because it is written right to left
entities.explanation: Because the verb comes last, so you wait for the whole sentence before you know the action.

entities.title: How many words for “you” does Hindi have?
entities.prompt: How many words for “you” does Hindi have?
entities.explanation: Three — आप (aap, respectful), तुम (tum, familiar) and तू (tu, intimate).

entities.title: Which word for “you” is the safe default with strangers?
entities.prompt: Which word for “you” is the safe default with strangers?
entities.explanation: आप (aap) is the respectful default; तुम (tum) is for friends and तू (tu) for very close intimates.

entities.title: What can choosing the wrong “you” do?
entities.prompt: What can choosing the wrong “you” do?
entities.explanation: Choosing wrong can be genuinely rude — the three words carry real social weight.

entities.title: Where do the mistakes in this guide come from?
entities.prompt: Where do the mistakes in this guide come from?
entities.answer: What actually goes wrong in lessons
options: What actually goes wrong in lessons
entities.explanation: The list is written from what actually goes wrong in lessons, not from a textbook.

entities.title: Why do learners find Hindi gender hard?
entities.prompt: Why do learners find Hindi gender hard?
entities.explanation: English nouns carry no gender, so remembering that every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine is a new habit.

entities.title: What marks a learner out fastest?
entities.prompt: What marks a learner out fastest?
entities.explanation: The errors that mark you out as a learner are the small, repeated ones — and each has a fix.

entities.title: Which half-hour words confuse every learner?
entities.prompt: Which half-hour words confuse every learner?
entities.explanation: ढाई (dhai, 2½) and साढ़े (saadhe, half past) — the half-hour words that confuse every learner.

entities.title: Which day is रविवार (ravivaar)?
entities.explanation: रविवार (ravivaar) is Sunday — named after Ravi, the sun.

entities.title: Which day is सोमवार (somvaar)?
entities.explanation: सोमवार (somvaar) is Monday — from som, the moon.

entities.title: What is your father's younger brother called?
entities.prompt: What is your father's younger brother called?
entities.explanation: चाचा (chaacha) is father's younger brother; ताऊ (taau) is father's older brother.

entities.title: What is your mother's brother called?
entities.prompt: What is your mother's brother called?
entities.explanation: मामा (maama) is mother's brother.

entities.title: Why is family vocabulary harder in Hindi than English?
entities.prompt: Why is family vocabulary harder in Hindi than English?
entities.answer: Hindi splits relations English lumps together
options: Hindi splits relations English lumps together
entities.explanation: Hindi splits relations English lumps together — like the two kinds of uncle — which is why there are more words to learn.

entities.title: What changes with the speaker's own gender?
entities.prompt: What changes with the speaker's own gender?
entities.explanation: Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine, and the verb changes with the speaker's own gender.

entities.title: Are all Hindi nouns gendered?
entities.answer: Yes — every noun is masculine or feminine
options: Yes — every noun is masculine or feminine
entities.explanation: Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine — there is no neuter.

entities.title: What helps you guess a noun's gender?
entities.prompt: What helps you guess a noun's gender?
options: Whether it is written in Devanagari
entities.explanation: Ending patterns — like -आ (-aa) often masculine and -ई (-ii) often feminine — let you guess most nouns.

entities.title: Why are Hindi numbers hard to learn?
entities.prompt: Why are Hindi numbers hard to learn?
options: There are too many of them
entities.explanation: Hindi numbers are genuinely irregular, unlike most languages.

entities.title: What is 11 in Hindi?
entities.explanation: ग्यारह (gyaarah) is 11; दस (das) is 10.

entities.title: What is 100 in Hindi?
entities.explanation: सौ (sau) is 100; हज़ार (hazaar) is 1,000.

entities.title: Can Hindi and Urdu speakers understand each other?
entities.prompt: Can Hindi and Urdu speakers understand each other?
entities.explanation: Hindi and Urdu speakers understand each other completely in everyday speech, yet the languages are treated as separate.

entities.title: What is the biggest visible difference between them?
entities.prompt: What is the biggest visible difference between them?
entities.explanation: Hindi is written in Devanagari and Urdu in a Perso-Arabic script; the spoken everyday language is very close.

entities.title: Where do the two vocabularies differ most?
entities.prompt: Where do the two vocabularies differ most?
entities.explanation: Formal and literary Hindi draws on Sanskrit while formal Urdu draws on Persian and Arabic; everyday words overlap heavily.

entities.title: What situations do the 50 phrases cover?
entities.prompt: What situations do the 50 phrases cover?
entities.answer: Bargaining, autos, trains, food, being unwell
options: Bargaining, autos, trains, food, being unwell
entities.explanation: Bargaining, autos, trains, food and being unwell — the situations that genuinely matter when travelling in India.

entities.title: Which phrase means “how much is this?”
entities.prompt: Which phrase means “how much is this?”
entities.answer: यह कितने का है? (yah kitne ka hai?)
options: यह कितने का है? (yah kitne ka hai?)
entities.explanation: यह कितने का है? (yah kitne ka hai?) is “how much is this?” — the bargaining essential.

entities.title: Why do numbers matter as much as phrases when you travel?
entities.prompt: Why do numbers matter as much as phrases when you travel?
entities.explanation: Prices are negotiated aloud, so numbers matter as much as phrases when you bargain.

entities.title: Which rule “catches everyone”?
entities.explanation: The ने (ne) rule — the ergative marker that appears with certain past-tense verbs — catches everyone.

entities.title: What do you need to conjugate a Hindi verb correctly?
entities.prompt: What do you need to conjugate a Hindi verb correctly?
entities.answer: Who is speaking, gender and tense
options: Who is speaking, gender and tense
entities.explanation: The verb ending depends on who is speaking, their gender and the tense.

entities.title: What does करना (karnaa) mean?
entities.explanation: करना (karnaa) means “to do” — the root verb used to build many others.

entities.title: Is Bollywood a good way to learn Hindi?
entities.prompt: Is Bollywood a good way to learn Hindi?
entities.answer: Yes — with the right films and method
options: Yes — with the right films and method
entities.explanation: Films are a genuinely good way to learn Hindi, if you pick the right ones and use them properly.

entities.title: What is the risk of learning from films alone?
entities.prompt: What is the risk of learning from films alone?
entities.explanation: Film dialogue is written for drama — songs and dramatic lines are not everyday speech.

entities.title: What should you pair films with?
entities.prompt: What should you pair films with?
entities.explanation: Films help most when paired with real conversation or structured study, so you learn which lines are actually used.

entities.title: What does this guide honestly compare?
entities.prompt: What does this guide honestly compare?
entities.explanation: A frank comparison of every way to learn Hindi online — apps, YouTube, textbooks and a tutor.

entities.title: What does the guide say about “learn Hindi in 30 days” promises?
entities.prompt: What does the guide say about “learn Hindi in 30 days” promises?
entities.explanation: The guide is frank that real fluency takes consistent months-to-years of work, not a month.

entities.title: Which real option does the guide compare?
entities.prompt: Which real option does the guide compare?
entities.explanation: The guide compares one-to-one tutoring, apps, YouTube and textbooks for what each is genuinely good for.

entities.title: What does this guide help you do?
entities.prompt: What does this guide help you do?
entities.answer: Write any English name in Devanagari
options: Write any English name in Devanagari
entities.explanation: Write any English name in Devanagari, letter by letter.

entities.title: What is Devanagari?
entities.answer: The script Hindi is written in
options: The script Hindi is written in
entities.explanation: Devanagari is the script Hindi is written in — an abugida where consonants carry an inherent “a”.

entities.title: Why can't English names always be written exactly?
entities.prompt: Why can't English names always be written exactly?
entities.explanation: Hindi letters represent sounds, so a name is written the way it sounds, not the way it is spelt in English.

entities.title: What does पानी mean?
entities.explanation: पानी (paani) is water — the word you will use most in India.

entities.title: What does रोटी mean?
entities.explanation: रोटी (roti) is the flat bread eaten with nearly every meal.

entities.title: What does चाय mean?
entities.explanation: चाय (chaay) is tea — and 'chai' is one of the few Hindi words the world already knows.

entities.title: What does घर mean?
entities.explanation: घर (ghar) is house or home.

entities.title: What does किताब mean?
entities.explanation: किताब (kitaab) is book — borrowed into Hindi from Arabic.

entities.title: What does दोस्त mean?
entities.explanation: दोस्त (dost) is friend.

entities.title: What does खाना mean?
entities.explanation: खाना (khaana) is food — also the verb 'to eat'.

entities.title: What does नमस्ते mean?
entities.explanation: नमस्ते (namaste) is hello — and also goodbye.

entities.title: What does धन्यवाद mean?
entities.explanation: धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad) is thank you. In speech people often say शुक्रिया (shukriya) instead.

entities.title: What does हाँ mean?
entities.explanation: हाँ (haan) is yes; नहीं (nahin) is no.

entities.title: What does बड़ा mean?
entities.explanation: बड़ा (bada) is big; छोटा (chhota) is small.

entities.title: What does अच्छा mean?
entities.explanation: अच्छा (achchha) is good. It also works as a filler word like 'okay'.

entities.title: What does पैसा mean?
entities.explanation: पैसा (paisa) is money — the word that gave English 'paisa'.

entities.title: What does स्कूल mean?
entities.explanation: स्कूल (skool) is school — a borrowing from English written in Devanagari.

entities.title: What does प्यार mean?
entities.explanation: प्यार (pyaar) is love.

entities.title: What does दिन mean?
entities.explanation: दिन (din) is day; रात (raat) is night.

entities.title: What does नया mean?
entities.explanation: नया (naya) is new.

entities.title: What does आदमी mean?
entities.explanation: आदमी (aadmi) is man; औरत (aurat) is woman.

entities.title: What does बच्चा mean?
entities.explanation: बच्चा (bachcha) is child.

entities.title: What does सुंदर mean?
entities.explanation: सुंदर (sundar) is beautiful.

entities.title: रोटी (bread) is which gender?
entities.explanation: Words ending in -ī (ई) are almost always feminine, like रोटी.

entities.title: घर (house) is which gender?
entities.explanation: घर ends in a consonant — the default is masculine.

entities.title: किताब (book) is which gender?
entities.explanation: किताब is feminine even though it ends in a consonant — an exception worth memorising.

entities.title: लड़का (boy) is which gender?
entities.explanation: Words ending in -ā (आ) like लड़का are masculine.

entities.title: The plural of लड़का (boy) is…
entities.explanation: Masculine -ā nouns change to -e in the direct plural: लड़का → लड़के.

entities.title: The plural of लड़की (girl) is…
entities.explanation: Feminine -ī nouns change to -iyaan in the direct plural: लड़की → लड़कियाँ.

entities.title: A man says: I go — मैं ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: A man says: I go — मैं ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: A male speaker uses the -aa ending: मैं जाता हूँ.

entities.title: A woman says: I go — मैं ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: A woman says: I go — मैं ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: A female speaker uses the -ii ending: मैं जाती हूँ.

entities.title: Present: मैं खाता हूँ means…
entities.explanation: मैं खाता हूँ is the habitual present: 'I eat'.

entities.title: Future: मैं खाऊँगा means…
entities.explanation: The -ūngā / -ūngī ending marks the future: मैं खाऊँगा, 'I will eat'.

entities.title: Past: मैंने खाया means…
entities.explanation: With transitive verbs the past uses ने and the -ā form agrees with the object: मैंने खाया, 'I ate (it)'.

entities.title: Which is correct for a woman: 'I am happy'?
entities.prompt: Which is correct for a woman: 'I am happy'?
entities.explanation: खुश doesn't change with gender; only the verb agrees: मैं … हूँ.

entities.title: Build: I eat bread
entities.explanation: Hindi is Subject–Object–Verb: I bread eat am.

entities.title: Build: She reads a book
entities.explanation: वह किताब पढ़ती है — subject, object, verb, auxiliary.

entities.title: Build: We live in Delhi
entities.explanation: दिल्ली में — 'Delhi in'. Postpositions come after the noun.

entities.title: Build: What is this?
entities.explanation: यह क्या है? — the question word sits just before the verb.

entities.title: Build: My name is Sita
entities.explanation: मेरा नाम सीता है — 'my name Sita is'.

entities.title: Build: I want tea
entities.explanation: मुझे चाय चाहिए — 'to me tea is wanted'.

entities.title: Build: Where do you live?
entities.explanation: आप कहाँ रहते हैं? — question word before the verb.

entities.title: Build: He goes to school
entities.explanation: वह स्कूल जाता है — subject, destination, verb.

entities.title: Build: I don't understand
entities.explanation: नहीं goes right before the verb: मैं नहीं समझता.

entities.title: Build: This is my house
entities.explanation: यह मेरा घर है — 'this my house is'.

entities.title: Build: I will go tomorrow
entities.explanation: मैं कल जाऊँगा — the verb stays last even in the future.

entities.title: Build: Give me water
entities.explanation: मुझे पानी दीजिए — the polite 'give' form.

entities.title: to go — a man says: मैं ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: to go — a man says: मैं ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: Male speaker, present: मैं जाता हूँ.

entities.title: to go — a woman says: मैं ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: to go — a woman says: मैं ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: Female speaker, present: मैं जाती हूँ.

entities.title: to eat — I will eat: मैं ____
entities.prompt: to eat — I will eat: मैं ____
entities.explanation: Future: मैं खाऊँगा.

entities.title: to be — I am: मैं ____
entities.explanation: मैं हूँ — 'I am'. है is he/she/it, हैं is they/you-polite.

entities.title: to be — he is: वह ____
entities.explanation: वह है — 'he/she is'.

entities.title: to do — a man: मैं काम ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: to do — a man: मैं काम ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: करना (to do) → मैं काम करता हूँ for a male speaker.

entities.title: to drink — she drinks tea: वह चाय ____ है
entities.prompt: to drink — she drinks tea: वह चाय ____ है
entities.explanation: पीना (to drink) → वह चाय पीती है (feminine).

entities.title: to come — you (polite) come: आप ____ हैं
entities.prompt: to come — you (polite) come: आप ____ हैं
entities.explanation: आप always takes the polite plural form: आप आते हैं.

entities.title: to speak — I speak Hindi: मैं हिंदी ____ हूँ
entities.prompt: to speak — I speak Hindi: मैं हिंदी ____ हूँ
entities.explanation: बोलना (to speak) → मैं हिंदी बोलता हूँ (male).

entities.title: to see — I saw: मैंने ____
entities.explanation: Past of देखना: मैंने देखा.

entities.title: You hear a greeting. What was it?
entities.prompt: You hear a greeting. What was it?
entities.explanation: नमस्ते is hello.

entities.title: You hear: water. Which word?
entities.explanation: पानी is water.

entities.title: You hear: thank you. Which word?
entities.prompt: You hear: thank you. Which word?
entities.explanation: धन्यवाद is thank you.

entities.title: You hear: how are you? Which phrase?
entities.prompt: You hear: how are you? Which phrase?
entities.explanation: आप कैसे हैं? — how are you (polite).

entities.title: You hear: my name is Ravi. Which phrase?
entities.prompt: You hear: my name is Ravi. Which phrase?
entities.explanation: मेरा नाम रवि है — my name is Ravi.

entities.title: You hear: yes. Which word?
entities.explanation: हाँ is yes.

entities.title: You hear: no. Which word?
entities.explanation: नहीं is no.

entities.title: You hear: I want tea. Which phrase?
entities.prompt: You hear: I want tea. Which phrase?
entities.explanation: मुझे चाय चाहिए — I want tea.

entities.title: You hear: goodbye. Which word?
entities.explanation: अलविदा is goodbye (from Arabic).

entities.title: You hear: good night. Which phrase?
entities.prompt: You hear: good night. Which phrase?
entities.explanation: शुभ रात्रि — good night.

entities.title: You hear: food. Which word?
entities.explanation: खाना is food.

entities.title: You hear: where are you from? Which phrase?
entities.prompt: You hear: where are you from? Which phrase?
entities.explanation: आप कहाँ से हैं? — where are you from?

entities.title: क vs ख — which has a puff of air?
entities.prompt: क vs ख — which has a puff of air?
entities.explanation: ख is aspirated — hold paper in front of your mouth and it moves.

entities.title: ग vs घ — which has a puff of air?
entities.prompt: ग vs घ — which has a puff of air?
entities.explanation: घ is the aspirated one.

entities.title: ट vs ठ — which is aspirated?
entities.prompt: ट vs ठ — which is aspirated?
entities.explanation: ठ is aspirated retroflex t.

entities.title: द vs ध — which is aspirated?
entities.prompt: द vs ध — which is aspirated?
entities.explanation: ध is aspirated d.

entities.title: ब vs भ — which is aspirated?
entities.prompt: ब vs भ — which is aspirated?
entities.explanation: भ is aspirated b.

entities.title: Which pair is: your tongue curls back (retroflex)?
entities.prompt: Which pair is: your tongue curls back (retroflex)?
entities.explanation: ट and ड are retroflex — tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth.

entities.title: Which pair is dental — tongue touching the teeth?
entities.prompt: Which pair is dental — tongue touching the teeth?
entities.explanation: त and द are dental — tongue against the back of the teeth.

entities.title: श vs स — which sounds like English 'sh'?
entities.prompt: श vs स — which sounds like English 'sh'?
entities.explanation: श is like 'sh' in 'ship'; स is like 's' in 'sun'.

entities.title: Can you read this word: नमस्ते
entities.prompt: Can you read this word: नमस्ते
options: I can sound out some letters
entities.explanation: If you read it instantly, the script is already yours. If you sounded it out, start with the alphabet guide anyway.

entities.title: Which means 'thank you'?
entities.explanation: धन्यवाद is thank you.

entities.title: Which word is 'water'?
entities.explanation: पानी is water.

entities.title: What is the correct order: I eat bread
entities.prompt: What is the correct order: I eat bread
entities.explanation: Subject–Object–Verb: मैं रोटी खाता हूँ.

entities.title: रोटी is which gender?
entities.explanation: रोटी is feminine.

entities.title: A woman says 'I go' — pick the right verb
entities.prompt: A woman says 'I go' — pick the right verb
entities.explanation: Female speaker: मैं जाती हूँ.

entities.title: Which is the future: 'I will eat'?
entities.prompt: Which is the future: 'I will eat'?
entities.explanation: मैं खाऊँगा is the future.

entities.title: Which is the polite 'you'?
entities.explanation: आप is the polite form, safe in almost every situation.

entities.title: What does कहाँ mean?
entities.explanation: कहाँ is where.

entities.title: Which number is 5 in Hindi?
entities.explanation: पाँच is five.

entities.title: I don't understand — which is right?
entities.prompt: I don't understand — which is right?
entities.explanation: नहीं goes right before the verb: मैं नहीं समझता.

entities.title: Can you hold a short conversation with a patient native speaker?
entities.prompt: Can you hold a short conversation with a patient native speaker?
entities.explanation: This is the one question a web page can't measure — be honest with yourself.

entities.title: मैं चाय पीता हूँ।
entities.explanation: चाय is tea, पीता हूँ is 'I drink' (male speaker).

entities.title: यह मेरा घर है।
entities.explanation: यह = this, मेरा घर = my house, है = is.

entities.title: वह बाज़ार जा रही है।
entities.answer: She is going to the market.
options: She is going to the market.
They are going to the market.
entities.explanation: जा रही है = 'is going' (female subject); बाज़ार = market.

entities.title: कल मौसम अच्छा था।
options: Tomorrow the weather will be nice.
entities.explanation: कल = yesterday, मौसम = weather, अच्छा था = was nice.

entities.title: मुझे हिन्दी सीखनी है।
entities.explanation: मुझे … है = 'I have to / I want to'; सीखनी = to learn.

entities.title: आपका नाम क्या है?
entities.explanation: आपका नाम = your name (polite), क्या है = what is.

entities.title: वह कल दिल्ली जाएगा।
entities.answer: He will go to Delhi tomorrow.
options: He will go to Delhi tomorrow.
entities.explanation: जाएगा = 'will go' (male); कल here = tomorrow.

entities.title: मुझे पानी चाहिए।
entities.explanation: चाहिए = need/want: मुझे पानी चाहिए.

entities.title: Which letter makes the sound 'ka' (as in car)?
entities.prompt: Which letter makes the sound 'ka' (as in car)?
entities.explanation: क is ka — the unaspirated k.

entities.title: Which letter is the vowel 'aa' (as in father)?
entities.prompt: Which letter is the vowel 'aa' (as in father)?
entities.explanation: आ is the long aa vowel.

entities.title: Which letter makes 'na' (dental)?
entities.explanation: न is dental na; ण is the retroflex na.

entities.title: Which letter is 'ma'?
entities.explanation: म is ma.

entities.title: Which letter makes 'ta' with the tongue curled back?
entities.prompt: Which letter makes 'ta' with the tongue curled back?
entities.explanation: ट is the retroflex ta; त is dental ta.

entities.title: Which letter is 'ha'?
entities.explanation: ह is ha.

entities.title: Which letter is the vowel 'i' (short)?
entities.explanation: इ is short i; ई is long ee.

entities.title: Which letter makes 'sa' (as in sun)?
entities.explanation: स is sa; श is sha (like ship).

entities.title: नमस्ते
entities.explanation: The universal greeting. The 't' is soft — nah-muh-stay, not nah-muh-STEE.

entities.title: धन्यवाद
entities.explanation: 'dh' is an aspirated d — a puff of air after the d.

entities.title: मेरा नाम ___ है
entities.answer: mera naam ___ hai — my name is ___
entities.explanation: Fill in your own name and say the whole sentence.

entities.title: आप कैसे हैं?
entities.answer: aap kaise hain? — how are you? (polite)
entities.explanation: The polite form — safe with anyone you don't know well.

entities.title: मुझे पानी चाहिए
entities.answer: mujhe paani chaahiye — I need water
entities.explanation: 'chaahiye' is the single most useful word for asking for things.

entities.title: यह कितने का है?
entities.answer: yah kitne ka hai? — how much is this?
entities.explanation: The essential market question. Practice until it's instant.

entities.title: मैं नहीं समझता हूँ
entities.answer: main nahin samajhta hoon — I don't understand
entities.explanation: A woman says 'samajhti'. Say the version that matches you.

entities.title: क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी बोलते हैं?
entities.answer: kya aap angrezi bolte hain? — do you speak English?
entities.explanation: 'kya' turns a statement into a yes/no question.

entities.title: मुझे मदद चाहिए
entities.answer: mujhe madad chaahiye — I need help
entities.explanation: Same 'chaahiye' pattern — pair it with anything you need.

entities.title: कल मिलेंगे
entities.explanation: 'phir milenge' (see you again) works too — the friendly goodbye.

entities.title: Hello / greetings
entities.usage_note: Neutral and safe with anyone. Not used between close friends, who mostly just say hi or the person's name.

entities.title: Hello (more formal)
entities.usage_note: A shade more formal than namaste. Common on television and in speeches.

entities.title: Good morning
entities.usage_note: Written and formal. In actual speech most people say namaste, or Good morning in English.

entities.title: How are you?
entities.usage_note: To a woman: आप कैसी हैं? (aap kaisi hain). The adjective agrees with the person you are addressing.

entities.title: How are you? (informal)
entities.usage_note: For friends and people younger than you. Using it with a stranger sounds abrupt.

entities.title: Goodbye
entities.usage_note: Heavier than English goodbye — it carries a sense of parting for a long time. Day to day, people say namaste again, or फिर मिलेंगे.

entities.title: See you later
entities.usage_note: we will meet again

entities.title: Good night
entities.usage_note: Formal. Good night in English is extremely common in speech.

entities.title: Thank you
entities.usage_note: Formal and sincere. Between friends and family Hindi often uses no thank-you at all; that is not rudeness, it is a different norm.

entities.title: Thanks (Urdu-origin, very common)
entities.usage_note: Lighter and warmer than dhanyavaad, and heard far more often in everyday speech.

entities.title: Please
entities.usage_note: Formal and mostly written. In speech, politeness is carried by the verb ending — कीजिए rather than a separate word for please.

entities.title: Sorry / excuse me
entities.usage_note: forgive (me)

entities.title: No problem
entities.usage_note: no matter at all

entities.title: Yes (polite)
entities.usage_note: जी is a respect particle. Adding it turns a blunt yes into a courteous one.

entities.title: Okay / I see
entities.usage_note: Also means good. As a response its meaning shifts with tone: agreement, mild surprise, or is that so.

entities.title: I am learning Hindi
entities.usage_note: A woman says सीख रही हूँ (seekh rahi hoon). Hindi verbs agree with the speaker's gender.

entities.title: I speak a little Hindi
entities.usage_note: A woman says बोलती हूँ (bolti hoon).

entities.title: How do you say this in Hindi?
entities.target_text: इसे हिंदी में क्या कहते हैं?
entities.romanization: ise hindi mein kya kehte hain
entities.meaning: How do you say this in Hindi?

entities.title: Where is the toilet?
entities.usage_note: बाथरूम is the word people actually use, borrowed from English. शौचालय exists but is signage Hindi.

entities.title: Please reduce the price a little
entities.meaning: Please reduce the price a little

entities.title: Please use the meter
entities.usage_note: Standard and expected in an auto-rickshaw. Saying it first, calmly, changes the negotiation.

entities.title: I am hungry
entities.usage_note: hunger has attached to me

entities.title: Not spicy, please
entities.usage_note: तीखा is chilli-hot. मसालेदार means well-spiced, which is not the same thing and is usually what you do want.

entities.title: I have eaten enough
entities.usage_note: Useful and often necessary. Refusing more food once is treated as politeness rather than a real answer.

entities.title: Father
entities.usage_note: पापा (papa) is what people actually call their father.

entities.title: Elder brother
entities.usage_note: बड़ा भाई for elder specifically. Also used for any man of similar age, affectionately.

entities.title: Elder sister
entities.usage_note: Widely used for any older woman you are friendly with, not only a sister.

entities.title: I like it
entities.usage_note: to me it is pleasing — the thing is the subject, not you

entities.title: I love you
entities.usage_note: A woman says करती हूँ (karti hoon). This is the film version; in real life people more often say it in English or not at all.

entities.title: I am tired
entities.usage_note: A woman: थक गई हूँ (thak gayi hoon).
